Irish Times, 24 October 2026

RewardsCompetitionsNewslettersWeather ForecastEuropePolice use tear gas and water cannons as more than 400,000 protest across FranceAuthorities had directed march away from centre of Paris to prevent repeat of last weekend’s violence and lootingA protester holds a French flag during a demonstration in Strasbourg, France, on Saturday. Photograph: Jean-Francois Badias/AP Thomas Adamson and Tom Nouvian, Associated PressSat Oct 24 2026 - 18:20 • 4 MIN READMore than 100,000 people have marched in Paris over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging president Emmanuel Macron’s government as police fired tear gas and water cannons near the end of the protest.

Paris police estimated the turnout at 110,000, with demonstrators mobilising despite restrictions that confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the centre.

Police used tear gas in several cities, including Lyons, Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported.

In Marseilles, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march’s endpoint. The Paris prosecutor’s office said 64 people had been arrested in connection with Saturday’s demonstration and 40 placed in police custody.

Those arrested included six minors.

Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offences or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.

The unrest is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for them.

[ Can Emmanuel Macron pull France back from the brink?Opens in new window ]

Interior minister Laurent Nuñez had announced a nationwide deployment of up to 70,000 officers, backed by helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons. Authorities had confined the Paris march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the centre.

An Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d’Italie early in the afternoon. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.

After reaching the authorised endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some demonstrators tried to continue towards Place de la Nation, but police blocked their path, French media reported.

Camille Chesnier, 27, said she had been unable to find work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.

“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.

Organisers from the “yellow vest” movement called for another day of protests on Saturday October 31st to defend the right to demonstrate.

Police changed the Paris route on Friday.

At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a €135 fine.

Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d’Italie.

“They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters,” she said.

“But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools.”

In Marseilles, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities.

Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyons, Nice and Montpellier. Trade unions have criticised the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.

Thousands also marched on Saturday in Orleans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.

[ The Irish Times view on protests in France: uncertainty and discontentOpens in new window ]

Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures restricting protests are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.

Nuñez acknowledged on Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend’s unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.

More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday, October 17th. Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over that weekend amid street violence not seen in years.

Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe on Saturday as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris.

The city’s main museums, including the Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais – where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display – were shut on Saturday.

Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public on Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend programme.

Paris protester Louis Ledoux-Xatard voiced frustration over inequality.

“Looking at countries like the United States, we don’t want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing,” he said.

“I never imagined that I’d be taking to the streets so much before my 30s.”

While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities on Saturday from Milan to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.

Thousands of young people marched through the streets of Milan, where large numbers of soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up in case of a repeat of last weekend’s chaotic looting and clashes.

Prime minister Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week.

In Albania’s capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police.

Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets on Saturday.

High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting against corruption in the education system.

Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of socialist prime minister Edi Rama.
